notes.enAnchorPrefix: And in the Gemara (Shabbat 88a)
notes.primary: Shabbat 88a: ‘Reish Lakish said: What is the meaning of that which is written, “And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day (yom ha-shishi)” (Genesis 1:31)? Why do I need the superfluous letter Hei in ha-shishi? This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, stipulated a condition with the works of creation and said to them: If Israel accepts the Torah on the sixth day of Sivan, you shall endure; and if not, I will return you to chaos and void (tohu va-vohu).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok opens Bereishit Ois 3 by contrasting the definite article Hei in ‘the sixth day’ (yom ha-shishi, Genesis 1:31) with the three occurrences of the definite article Hei in ‘on the seventh day’ (ba-yom ha-shevi’i, Genesis 2:2–3). While ‘the sixth day’ alludes to the sixth of Sivan according to the lunar calendar sanctified by Israel from below, ‘the seventh day’ alludes to the Sabbath day on which the Torah was given according to the immutable seven-day cycle fixed by Hashem from Above.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: concerning that which is stated 'the sixth day' (Genesis 1:31):
notes.primary: Genesis 1:31: ‘And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day (yom ha-shishi).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: The anomalous addition of the definite article Hei to ‘sixth’ (yom ha-shishi, rather than yom shishi as on the preceding days) links the completion of the six days of Creation to the specific sixth day of Sivan when Israel stood at Sinai.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: as written (there, Shabbat 86b):
notes.primary: Shabbat 86b: ‘The Sages taught in a Baraita: On the sixth day of the month of Sivan the Ten Commandments were given to Israel; Rabbi Yosi says: On the seventh day of Sivan. Rava said: Everyone agrees (de-khulei alma) that the Torah was given to Israel on Shabbat; where they differ is only regarding how the New Moon of Sivan was fixed that year.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok cites Rava’s rule in Shabbat 86b (‘Everyone agrees that the Torah was given to Israel on Shabbat’) to resolve the three extra letters Hei in ha-shevi’i (‘the seventh day’): just as ha-shishi points to Matan Torah from Israel’s perspective (the sixth of Sivan, established by the earthly court’s sanctification of the moon), ha-shevi’i points to Matan Torah from God’s perspective (the cosmic Sabbath day, whose sanctity is fixed and independent of human calculation).

notes.enAnchorPrefix: And it is written: 'And God finished on the seventh day' (Genesis 2:2),
notes.primary: Genesis 2:2: ‘And on the seventh day God finished (va-yekhal) His work which He had made; and He rested (va-yishbot) on the seventh day from all His work which He had made.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok analyzes the three verbs attached to the seventh day in Genesis 2:2–3—va-yekhal (‘He finished / yearned’), va-yishbot (‘He rested’), and va-yevarekh (‘He blessed’)—showing how each corresponds to one of the three mentions of ha-shevi’i and one of the three levels of Sabbath holiness.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה י, ט):
notes.enAnchorPrefix: in accordance with what is written in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 10:9):
notes.primary: Bereshit Rabbah 10:9: ‘“And on the seventh day God finished His work” (Genesis 2:2): Geniba and the Rabbis expounded: Like a king who made a bridal chamber—as long as the bride has not entered it, what does the chamber lack? It lacks the bride! Similarly, what did the world lack after the six days? It lacked Shabbat: once Shabbat arrived, rest and completion arrived (ba’at Shabbat, ba’at menuchah).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok interprets the Midrashic statement ‘Shabbat arrived—rest arrived’ as referring to the inner serenity and delight (niyucha) experienced by the Creator Himself in His world when foreseeing that Israel would receive the Torah on Shabbat.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and as written (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 9:
notes.primary: Bereshit Rabbah 9: ‘Rabbi Levi said: To what may this be compared? To a king who built a palace and beheld it completed and adorned; he exclaimed: “O palace, My palace! Would that you always find grace and favor before Me at all times just as you have found favor before Me at this hour!” Similarly, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to His world at the completion of Creation: “O My world, My world! Would that you find favor before Me at all times just as you have found favor before Me at this hour!”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: This Midrashic exclamation (‘My world, My world!’) reveals what ‘rest’ (menuchah) means with respect to God: not cessation from fatigue, Heaven forbid, but the Creator’s joyous satisfaction when His creation fulfills its inner purpose through Israel’s acceptance of the Torah.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: which the Targum Yerushalmi translates as: 'and He yearned/cherished,'
notes.primary: Targum Jerusalem on Genesis 2:2: ‘In Targum Yerushalmi on Genesis 2:2, the word va-yekhal (“and He finished”) is rendered va-chamid (“and He desired / cherished,” from the root kalah, yearning of the soul, as in “My soul yearns [kaltah] for Your salvation”); and Abudarham notes that for this reason the Sabbath prayer calls Shabbat chemdat ha-yamim (“the coveted / cherished of all days”).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: By linking va-yekhal to divine yearning and delight (va-chamid / chemdat ha-yamim), Rav Tzadok shows that the first occurrence of ‘on the seventh day’ expresses Hashem’s love and longing for Knesset Yisrael, who would receive the Torah on Shabbat.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּדְרַשׁ (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה ט)
notes.enAnchorPrefix: just as expounded (Bereishit Rabbah there, parashah 9)
notes.primary: Bereshit Rabbah 9:4: ‘In the Torah scroll of Rabbi Meir they found written on “And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good (tov me’od)” (Genesis 1:31): “and behold, death was good”—and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman said: “Behold, it was very good” refers to the Evil Inclination (Yetzer HaRa), as well as suffering and Gehinnom, for through them man is spurred to return to God.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok connects the word kol (‘from all [mi-kol] His work’) in the second clause of Vayechulu with the word kol in Genesis 1:31 (‘all [et kol] that He had made, and behold, it was very good’): through the Torah given on Shabbat, even the forces that appear opposite to goodness—such as the Evil Inclination—are ultimately transformed into ‘very good.’

notes.heAnchorPrefix: עַל "אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד"
notes.enAnchorPrefix: – on the verse 'all that He had made, and behold, it was very good' (Genesis 1:31)
notes.primary: Genesis 1:31: ‘And God saw all (et kol) that He had made, and behold, it was very good (tov me’od).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: While each individual day’s creation was pronounced ‘good’ (tov), the all-encompassing vista of ‘all that He had made’ (et kol asher asah)—which includes the adversarial forces of darkness and the Evil Inclination—is pronounced ‘very good’ (tov me’od) when rectified through the Torah.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: And so it is written (Isaiah 45:7):
notes.primary: Isaiah 45:7: ‘I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil (u-vorei ra); I the Lord do all these things.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Scripture explicitly testifies in Isaiah 45:7 that the Creator Himself formed darkness and evil so that they may ultimately serve the revelation of light and peace.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: yet we recite in the liturgy: 'Who forms all,' using a euphemistic phrasing (Berakhot 11b),
notes.primary: Berakhot 11b: ‘In the prophet Isaiah it is written: “Who forms light and creates darkness, who makes peace and creates evil” (Isaiah 45:7); yet in the morning blessing before Shema we recite: “Who makes peace and creates all things (ha-kol),” employing a refined, euphemistic expression (lishna ma’alya).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok points out that the Talmud’s substitution of ha-kol (‘all things’) for ra (‘evil’) in Berakhot 11b is not merely verbal politeness: it reveals that the word kol (‘all’) in ‘He rested from all (mi-kol) His work’ specifically encompasses the opposite of good, which is elevated into holiness through the Torah of Shabbat.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: וְהוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר אוֹר הַחַיִּים (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב, ב),
notes.enAnchorPrefix: And this aligns with what is written in the holy Ohr HaChayim (Genesis 2:2),
notes.primary: Or HaChaim on Genesis 2:2:1: ‘Rabbi Chaim ibn Attar (Ohr HaChaim on Genesis 2:2–3) explains that during the six days of Creation, the Holy One, blessed be He, endowed the universe with only enough spiritual life-force to endure for six days; when Shabbat arrives, the Creator infuses a new soul and fresh vitality into the world on every Shabbat, empowering creation to exist for another six days—and this is the meaning of “And God blessed the seventh day,” that it continually generates blessing and existence for the six workdays.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok cites the Ohr HaChaim to explain the third mention of ‘the seventh day’ (‘And God blessed the seventh day’): because ‘blessing’ (berakhah) always signifies increase and reproduction, the blessing of Shabbat—activated by Israel’s acceptance of the Torah on Shabbat—continually gives birth to the spiritual vitality of the six ensuing weekdays.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and in accordance with what is written (Shabbat 89b):
notes.primary: Shabbat 89b: ‘In the Time to Come, the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to Isaac: Your children have sinned against Me! Isaac will reply before Him: Master of the Universe, even if a person lived seventy or eighty years, how many years could he actually sin once sleep, childhood, prayer, and bodily needs are subtracted? And if You will bear the sin, bear it all! Thereupon Israel will declare to Isaac: “For You are our father!” and Rava expounded: “Though your sins be as scarlet (ka-shanim), they shall become white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18)—even if your sins are ingrained like these years (shanim) that have been ordered and continuous from the six days of Creation until now, they shall become white as snow!’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok maps the three clauses of Vayechulu onto the three supernal heads of Shabbat: Va-yekhal corresponds to the Friday night meal of Chakal Tapuchin Kadishin (Malkhut, revealing that Israel’s souls are intrinsically pure ‘apples’); Va-yishbot mi-kol melakhto corresponds to the Sabbath day meal of Atika Kadisha (Keter, the primordial utterance of Bereishit), where through repentance out of love even the sins ordered from the six days of Creation (‘ka-shanim’) are whitened into snow and revealed as part of the primordial design.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: וָא״ו דְּאִקְרֵי אוֹת אֱמֶת (זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיִּקְרָא),
notes.enAnchorPrefix: the letter Vav which is termed the 'sign of truth' (holy Zohar, start of Parashat Vayikra),
notes.primary: Zohar, Vayikra 2:10: ‘At the beginning of Parashat Vayikra (Zohar III 2a), the letter Vav (whose numerical value is six) is expounded as the “Sign of Truth” (Ot Emet), corresponding to Ze’ir Anpin (the Holy One, blessed be He, and the attribute of Jacob), which channels supernal blessing into the six directions of the world.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok links the third clause (‘And God blessed the seventh day’) to the third Sabbath meal (Seudah Shelishit), corresponding to Ze’ir Anpin—the letter Vav, the ‘Sign of Truth’—which draws the eternal truth of Shabbat into the six days of the coming week.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and it is written (Proverbs 12:19):
notes.primary: Proverbs 12:19: ‘The lip of truth shall be established forever (sefat emet tikon la’ad), but a lying tongue is but for a moment.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Because Ze’ir Anpin (the attribute of Jacob and the Written Torah, represented by the letter Vav) is the attribute of Truth (‘You give truth to Jacob’), the blessing drawn down from Shabbat through Vayevarekh endures forever and sustains the six weekdays in holiness.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: וּמַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית נִקְרָא "כֹּחַ מַעֲשָׂיו הִגִּיד לְעַמּוֹ",
notes.enAnchorPrefix: and the Work of Creation is termed 'the power of His works He declared to His people' (Psalms 111:6),
notes.primary: Psalms 111:6: ‘He has declared to His people the power of His works (koach ma’asav higid le-amo), in giving them the heritage of the nations’ (Psalms 111:6)—cited by Rashi on Genesis 1:1 from Midrash Tanchuma and Bereshit Rabbah 1:2 to explain why the Torah opens with the account of Creation. Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok explains why the Divine Name Elohim (‘Master of all forces,’ ba’al ha-kochot kulam) appears three times in Vayechulu: in Va-yekhal Elohim and Va-yevarekh Elohim, the Name Elohim signifies that even the human awakening from below (itaruta de-letata) by which Israel sanctifies Shabbat is itself a power granted to Israel by Hashem.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: שֶׁהוּא "אַתָּה הוּא עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, אַתָּה הוּא מִשֶּׁנִּבְרָא הָעוֹלָם".
notes.enAnchorPrefix: the level of 'You were He before the world was created, You are He after the world was created.'
notes.primary: Yoma 69b: ‘In the morning liturgy (and cf. Yoma 69b on the Men of the Great Assembly restoring God’s crowns): “You were He (Atah Hu) before the world was created; You are He (Atah Hu) since the world was created”—signifying the absolute, unchanging unity of Atika Kadisha above all division between good and evil.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In the middle clause—‘and He rested (va-yishbot) on the seventh day from all His work’—the Name Elohim is omitted! Rav Tzadok explains that this is because the rectification of ‘from all His work’ (transforming evil itself into good) stems from Atika Kadisha, the transcendent realm of ‘You were He before the world was created,’ where no opposing force ever existed independently.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: כִּי בוֹ שָׁבַת מִכָּל מְלַאכְתּוֹ אֲשֶׁר בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים לַעֲשׂוֹת",
notes.enAnchorPrefix: 'because that in it He rested from all His work which God created to make' (Genesis 2:3),
notes.primary: Genesis 2:3: ‘And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it; because that in it He rested from all His work which God created to make (asher bara Elohim la’asot).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: The third occurrence of the Name Elohim appears at the very end of Vayechulu—‘which God (Elohim) created to make (la’asot)’—teaching that when the transcendent light of Atika descends into the lower world of Elohim, it empowers human beings (‘to make’) to transform darkness into light.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק ב, קפד עַמּוּד א).
notes.enAnchorPrefix: (holy Zohar, Part II, 184a).
notes.primary: Zohar, Tetzaveh 10:83-11:92: ‘In the Zohar (Tetzaveh II 184a), Rabbi Shimon expounds: “Why did the Holy One, blessed be He, send Israel down into the darkness of exile? Because there is no true light except that which emerges from within darkness (de-leit nehora ela hahu de-nafik mi-go chashokha), and there is no true good except that which is recognized from within evil (ve-leit tava ela hahu de-nafik mi-go bisha).”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: This foundational Zoharic principle explains why Hashem derives satisfaction even from what appears opposite to the good: from the very first utterance of Creation, the Supernal Thought ordained that darkness precede light so that when man overcomes darkness through repentance out of love, a far higher light shines forth.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and as written (Bereishit Rabbah, parashah 11:
notes.primary: Bereshit Rabbah 11: ‘“Which God created to make (la’asot)” (Genesis 2:3): Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said: Everything that was created during the six days of Creation requires further human preparation and action—for example, mustard needs to be sweetened, lupines need to be sweetened, wheat needs to be ground and baked, and even man himself requires rectification (tikkun) through circumcision and the commandments.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok reads the infinitive la’asot (‘to make’) at the close of Vayechulu through Bereshit Rabbah 11:6: God deliberately left creation unfinished so that human beings would become active partners in rectifying and sweetening both the physical world and their own souls.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and this is derived from the word 'to make' (la'asot), as Rashi explained,
notes.primary: Rashi on Genesis 2:3:2: ‘Rashi on Genesis 2:3 (“which God created to make”): The work that was worthy of being done on Shabbat He doubled and did on the sixth day, as is explained in Bereshit Rabbah; and midrashically, “to make” (la’asot) teaches that everything created in the six days requires human completion and repair thereafter.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rashi’s comment on la’asot underscores that the culmination of Creation is entrusted to human labor in Torah and mitzvot.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and so is written in Midrash Tanchuma (Parashat Tazria 5)
notes.primary: Midrash Tanchuma, Tazria 5: ‘Turnus Rufus the wicked asked Rabbi Akiva: “Whose works are more beautiful, those of the Holy One, blessed be He, or those of flesh and blood?” Rabbi Akiva replied: “Those of flesh and blood are more beautiful!” When Turnus Rufus challenged him over circumcision, Rabbi Akiva brought him stalks of wheat and fine baked cakes of bread, saying: “These stalks are the work of the Holy One, blessed be He, and these cakes are the work of flesh and blood—are not the cakes finer?” Turnus Rufus said: “If God desires circumcision, why does the infant not emerge circumcised from his mother’s womb?” Rabbi Akiva answered: “Because the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the commandments to Israel solely in order to refine and purify them through their own action!”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok cites Rabbi Akiva’s famous disputation with Turnus Rufus in Tanchuma Tazria 5 to prove that human effort in rectifying oneself—symbolized by circumcision and repentance out of love—is precisely what makes creation most beautiful before Hashem.

notes.heAnchorPrefix: שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא פו.),
notes.enAnchorPrefix: so that willful sins are transformed into merits as taught (Yoma 86a),
notes.primary: Yoma 86b: ‘Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, for through it willful sins (zedonot) are accounted to a person as actual merits (zekhuyot), as it is stated: “When the wicked turns from his wickedness, and does that which is lawful and right, he shall live by them (aleihem)” (Ezekiel 33:19)—on account of those very deeds he shall live! And this applies specifically to repentance motivated by love (teshuvah me-ahavah).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Through repentance out of love (Yoma 86b), the human task of la’asot (‘to make’) reaches its pinnacle: past transgressions are not merely erased, but are transformed into vessels of yearning and merit, fulfilling ‘they shall become white as snow.’

notes.enAnchorPrefix: And as written in Midrash Tanchuma (there): "
notes.primary: Midrash Tanchuma, Tazria 5: ‘“And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31): The Holy One, blessed be He, said to man: “Why do you call the Evil Inclination evil? It is you who make it evil! Behold, a small child cannot guard himself, yet once you grow up you have the power to rule over it. How many bitter and harsh herbs exist in the world—such as mustard, capers, and lupines—that are far more bitter than the Evil Inclination, yet you know how to boil and sweeten them for your benefit! How much more so can you sweeten the Evil Inclination through the Torah!”’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Just as human beings sweeten bitter mustard and lupines, man is charged with sweetening the bitter drive of the Evil Inclination through Torah and repentance out of love, thereby bringing divine satisfaction (niyucha) from the very opposite of good.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: 'And your people are all righteous' (Isaiah 60:21),
notes.primary: Isaiah 60:21: ‘And your people, all of them righteous (ve-amekha khulam tzaddikim), shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, wherein I may be glorified.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Rav Tzadok concludes Bereishit Ois 3 with an overarching promise: while the protracted exile is designed so that every Jewish soul may achieve rectification from its own initiative through teshuvah me-ahavah (under the Name Elohim in ‘created to make’), even if a person fails to complete that clarification on his own, in the ultimate future the transcendent light of Atika Kadisha (where the Name Elohim is absent in ‘and He rested from all His work’) will shine forth and purify every Jew.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: and whoever is circumcised is designated righteous,
notes.primary: Zohar, Lech Lecha 93a: ‘In the Zohar (Lech Lecha I 93a), on “And your people are all righteous” (Isaiah 60:21), Rabbi Abba teaches: Because Israel bring their infant sons on the eighth day to enter the covenant of Abraham, whoever is sealed with the sign of the holy Covenant is called Tzaddik (Righteous) and is bound at his root to the World to Come.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: Because every Jew bears the seal of the Covenant at the root of his soul (‘whoever is circumcised is called righteous’), his inner point of holiness remains eternally intact even amidst the stumbles of exile.

notes.enAnchorPrefix: for 'none cast out shall be permanently expelled from Him.'
notes.primary: II Samuel 14:14: ‘For we must needs die, and are as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again; neither does God take away life, but devises thoughts so that he that is banished be not an outcast from Him (le-vilti yidach mimenu nidach).’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: From the supernal vantage point of Atika Kadisha—the Sabbath of the World to Come—‘no banished soul shall remain cast away from Him’ (II Samuel 14:14), for every Jewish soul will ultimately be restored to complete holiness.
